machine-learning.text: A machine learning model is a program you did not write line by line. You supply examples, and an algorithm searches for a rule that fits them and, more importantly, holds up on examples it has never seen. That second part is the whole difficulty, and it is why this pathway is shaped the way it is. Six sections: what learning from data actually means, the classical algorithm families and when each earns its place, how models are trained, how to evaluate them honestly, what you can do without labels, and what breaks once a model is serving real traffic.
machine-learning.deep_text:
The order here is deliberate. Foundations of Learning comes first because almost every mistake later in the pathway is a foundations mistake wearing a costume — a leaked feature, a test set consulted too often, a model with more capacity than the data can support. Once you can say precisely why minimising training error is not the goal, the rest of the pathway stops looking like a catalogue of tricks and starts looking like a set of answers to one question.

Supervised Learning Algorithms then walks the families in rough order of assumption strength: linear models, which assume a great deal and are correspondingly cheap and interpretable; tree ensembles, which assume very little about shape and dominate most tabular problems in practice; distance and margin methods; and neural networks, taken only as far as the perceptron, hidden layers, and backpropagation. Training and Optimisation sits next because it explains the machinery those algorithms share — gradient descent, feature preparation, hyperparameter search — rather than repeating it inside each one.

Evaluation and Model Selection is placed fourth but is the section experienced practitioners return to most. A model is only as trustworthy as the number you used to choose it, and accuracy is usually the wrong number. Unsupervised and Semi-Supervised Learning then relaxes the assumption that labels exist at all, covering clustering, dimensionality reduction, and the ways of squeezing value out of a small labelled set. Machine Learning in Production closes the loop: serving, drift, monitoring, fairness, and reproducibility.

What this pathway does not do: it does not teach deep learning architectures beyond the basics, which belong to the Deep Learning pathway; it does not cover large language models, transformers, or generative AI, which belong to the LLMs and Generative AI pathway; it does not cover RAG or agent engineering, owned by AI Engineering; and it does not build data pipelines or warehouses, owned by Data Engineering. Everything here is the layer those pathways assume you already have.
